transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in today?

Well, I’m here because everyone keeps telling me this is just about the foreclosure, like it’s just paperwork and missed payments and procedures, and I’m supposed to just accept that. But that’s not what’s been happening. I know what I’ve been seeing.

For almost two years now, it’s been like the bank and the loan servicer are not just doing their normal job. They’ve been working together, and I’m pretty sure people at my job have gotten pulled into it too, quietly, behind the scenes. It’s like they’re all trying to push me out of my house, and then they act like I’m the one making it complicated when I ask questions or point out things that don’t add up.

They keep showing me papers, letters, statements, all these official-looking documents, and everyone says, “See, this explains it.” But no amount of papers changes what I’ve actually been seeing. The timing of things, the way people talk around me, the way certain things happen right after I say something at work or after I call the servicer—it’s not random. I know people want me to believe it’s just missed payments, but it’s bigger than that. That’s why I came in, because I’m tired of being treated like I’m not seeing what’s right in front of me.
Aside from these suspicions about being watched or targeted, have you ever heard voices, sounds, or seen things that other people don't seem to notice?

No, not like voices talking to me or anything like that. I mean, I notice things other people say they don’t notice, but that’s different. Like patterns, timing, the way people look over or stop talking when I come near—that kind of thing. 

But if you mean hearing a voice when nobody’s there, or seeing a person or something that other people can’t see, then no, I don’t think so. I’m not saying I’ve never misheard a noise in the house or thought I heard something outside, because everybody does that, especially when you’re stressed. But I’m not hearing voices or seeing things that aren’t there. That’s not what this is.

Over this same two-year period, have you noticed significant changes in your mood—such as feeling unusually depressed, hopeless, or on the other hand, unusually elevated, energetic, or needing much less sleep than normal?

I don’t know how to answer that exactly. I mean, anybody would feel worn down after dealing with something like this for this long. There are days I feel frustrated, or upset, or like I’m just tired of having to explain myself over and over when people already decided what they want to believe. But I wouldn’t say it’s like I just woke up one day and became a completely different person mood-wise.

As far as being “unusually elevated” or energized, no, not really. I’m not walking around feeling amazing or invincible or anything like that. And with sleep, I mean, if I’m thinking about what’s going on, of course it can be harder to settle down, but I don’t know that I’d call it needing less sleep in that way you’re asking. It’s more just having a lot on my mind.

Depressed or hopeless… I don’t know. I get discouraged, sure. I get angry. I get tired of it. But I still go to work, I still do what I have to do. So I guess I’d say I haven’t noticed some big mood change separate from the situation. It’s more that the situation is exhausting.

Before this situation with the foreclosure started, would you say you've generally been a very trusting person with friends, family, and coworkers, or have you always tended to be wary and suspicious of other people's motives, even in unrelated parts of your life?

I mean… I don’t know if I’d call myself “very trusting.” That sounds kind of naive, and I don’t think I’ve ever been naive. I work in retail supervision, so you learn pretty quickly that people have reasons for what they do, and sometimes they say one thing and mean another. But that’s not the same as thinking everyone is out to get me.

Before all this, I think I was probably normal about people? Like, with friends and family, if something felt off, I might notice it, but I wasn’t sitting around connecting everything or assuming there was some bigger thing going on. At work, I pay attention because I have to—who’s reliable, who’s trying to avoid responsibility, who’s saying things just to cover themselves. That’s part of the job. But I wouldn’t say I was suspicious of everybody in every area of my life.

So… I guess I’m not sure how to answer it cleanly. I wasn’t someone who just blindly trusted people, but I also don’t think I walked around thinking people had hidden motives all the time. This feels different because there are actual things that happened that made me start questioning people.

Have you had any recent medical issues, head injuries, new medications, or substance use—or noticed any changes in your memory, concentration, or physical health—around the time these beliefs started?

I don’t think so. I mean, not that I can point to. I haven’t had some head injury or accident where everything changed afterward, if that’s what you mean. And I’m not on some new medication that started right before all this, at least nothing that stands out to me like that.

Substance use… no, nothing unusual. I mean, I’m not saying I’ve lived in a bubble my whole life, but there wasn’t some new drug thing or drinking thing that lined up with it. That’s not really part of this.

As far as memory or concentration, I guess it depends what you mean. When you’re under stress and trying to keep track of everything, you can feel distracted, but I don’t think my memory just suddenly got bad or anything. I can do my job, I can keep up with schedules and responsibilities. Sometimes I replay things in my head a lot because I’m trying to understand what happened, and then people act like that means I’m not concentrating, but I am concentrating—just on something they don’t want to talk about.

Physically, I don’t know. I’ve been tired at times, but again, that seems pretty normal considering everything. I can’t think of some medical problem that started right then and explains it. So, no, nothing obvious like that.
Do you have any diagnosed medical conditions—such as thyroid problems, autoimmune diseases, seizures, or other neurological issues—that a doctor has told you about?

Not that I’ve been told, no. I mean, I’ve had regular doctor visits here and there like anyone, but no one has sat me down and said I have a thyroid condition or seizures or some neurological disease or anything like that.

I guess I don’t always know what counts as “autoimmune” unless somebody specifically tells you, but as far as I know, no. I haven’t been diagnosed with something like that. If there were something in my chart that I’m forgetting, I’d be surprised, because I think I would remember a doctor making a big deal out of it.

So… no, not that I know of.
Have you noticed any episodes of confusion, feeling disoriented, or fluctuations in your level of alertness—like moments where you felt foggy or unsure of where you were or what was happening?

No, I don’t think so. Not in the way you’re describing, like not knowing where I am or what’s happening. I’ve never had that thing where you wake up somewhere and don’t understand how you got there, or suddenly can’t recognize a place, or people are saying I seemed “out of it” and I don’t remember it. Nothing like that.

I mean, I can feel mentally overloaded sometimes, sure, but that’s different to me. If I’m thinking through a lot at once, or if I’m trying to remember exactly what someone said or what order things happened in, I might seem quiet or distracted. But I know where I am. I know what day it is, I know what I’m doing. I’m not confused like… medically confused, if that makes sense.

And foggy—again, I don’t know. People use that word for everything. If I’m tired or stressed, I might feel like I need a minute to get my thoughts straight, but I wouldn’t call it being disoriented. I haven’t noticed my alertness going up and down in some strange way. It’s more that I’m focused on certain things, and when other people don’t want to deal with those things, they act like I’m not paying attention. But I am paying attention. So no, I don’t think I’ve had episodes like that.

There is no evidence of hallucinations, disorganized speech/behavior, or negative symptoms typical of schizophrenia.
